The first thing I usually do when I go to check out videos on the topic of GMOs is read the description of the video. In this case it states:

Genetically modified (GM) foods have been around for decades. Created by modifying the DNA of one organism through the introduction of genes from another, they are developed for a number of different reasons-to fight disease, enhance flavor, resist pests, improve nutrition, survive drought-and are mainly found in our food supply in processed foods using corn, soybeans, and sugar beets, and as feed for farm animals. Across the country and around the world, communities are fighting the cultivation of genetically engineered crops. Are they safe? How do they impact the environment? Can they improve food security? Is the world better off with or without GM food?

Three things immediately stand out to me there:

  1. They're leaving out the single biggest use for GMOs today which is to increase their resistance to various poisons. The organisms are modified to enable farmers to spray them with poisons that are toxic to plants and animals alike so the farmers can kill everything except the plant itself with minimal effort. The primary active ingredient (glyphosphate) in the main poison they're modified to be resistant to was just last week also declared a probable carcinogen, or cancer causing agent, by the World Health Organization.

  2. I think it's also misleading to say GMOs have been in use for decades. It's not untrue, yet the implication is different than reality which is they only first began production in the 80s and 90s and it took quite some time from there for them to become ubiquitous in countres like the US as they are today. When you think decades, most people are probably not going to realize that "we" are the first generation to have been ingesting GMOs throughout our developmental period. You generally use terms like that when you're trying to convince people that they've been in use longer than they have without actually lying.

  3. Finally they also do not distinguish GMOs from cross breeding. They're not the same thing. Cross breeding requires closely related species. Genetic modification is primarily the realm of mixing traits from species which are in no way related. It's not like making a mule out of a donkey and a horse. It's more akin to forging the mythological chimera - an organism with the head of a lion, body of a goat and tail of a snake. The consequences of this action are completely unexplored, not only because it's such a new field but also because the primary players in GMOs have been legally allowed to prevent open and unrestricted research on their organisms thanks to patents. Fortunately the first patent on the biggest name in GMOs just expired this month so we may see some purely independent research coming out it in the years to follow.

Anyhow, like I said that's not necessarily a judgement on the video yet but the description is certainly what I'd expect from a biased individual.

edit I'd also add that at least among individuals who aren't emotionally swinging one way or the other, one of the biggest concerns with GMOs today isn't directly GMOs but the companies with an effective monopoly on their production and use. While ideally the debate about GMOs should be independent of the companies involved with them, the reality is that it's an integral part of the issue. There's a small handful of companies dominating the market and they in turn are almost exclusively using product derivatives of one company - Monsanto. That company has an abhorrent history of ethical breaches and putting profit above absolutely everything, including lives. They make the much more well known name Comcast seem like angels by comparison. They've also managed to openly and legally infiltrate the government agencies that are supposedly regulating them. Among other roles, they've managed to get a Monsanto VP/lobbyist appointed as the deputy commissioner for foods at the FDA.

The carcinogenic active ingredient I mentioned above, glyphosphate? Monsanto recently successfully lobbied the USDA to increase the allowed maximum residue of. And, quoting that Reuter's article:

As has been the case with past analyses, the USDA said it did not test this past year for residues of glyphosate, the active ingredient in Roundup herbicide and the world's most widely used herbicide. A USDA spokesman who asked not to be quoted said that the test measures required for glyphosate are "extremely expensive... to do on an regular basis".

There are just egregious conflicts of interest and potential ethical breeches abound when it comes to GMOs. While I support GMOs from a theoretic point of view, from a practical point of view I think it'd clearly be in the best interest of everybody if that industry was simply disabled until it could be reformed and rebooted.

With regards to part of your point 1, AFIK that yes, some GMO's may be resistant against some of the man-made chemicals that are used in agriculture, in some/many? cases this actually allows for less overall man-made chemical usage, as a blend of chemicals can be replaced with the single one. If that's better or worse, I suppose it would depend on if my AFIK is A: right, and B: what you are replacing what with.
